name: Team error
statement: Team error is a label for a mistake the team around it failed to catch, drawn from incident classification rather than from any experiment that measures it.
meaning: Kunihide Sasou and James Reason gave the term its current use, and their argument starts as a complaint about method. Error analysis usually looks at the individual who made the error. In large complex systems most people work in teams or groups, so the unit of analysis is wrong. They proposed a definition of team errors and a taxonomy for them, then applied both to events in the nuclear power, aviation and shipping industries. Their conclusion names four conditions that will cause team errors: deficiencies in communication, deficiencies in resource and task management, an excessive authority gradient, and excessive professional courtesy. The point of the relabelling is practical. Handling human errors as team errors, they write, provides an opportunity to reduce human errors. The categories inside the taxonomy are not set out here, because the paper is paywalled and only its abstract could be read.

origin.note: The paper is 'Team errors: definition and taxonomy', volume 65, issue 1, pages 1 to 9, published in June 1999. Sasou was at the Human Factors Research Center of the Central Research Institute of Electric Power Industry in Tokyo and Reason at the University of Manchester, according to the affiliations held in the Unpaywall record. The abstract also says the paper relates team errors to Performance Shaping Factors.

evidence: The evidence under the label is incident review, and it reads as such. The Joint Commission's 2024 annual review covers 1,575 sentinel events reported by American healthcare organisations during that year. Team failures appear in its lists of contributing factors. Of the 1,472 factors recorded for unintended retention of a foreign object, a lack of shared understanding or mental model across the care team accounts for 14 per cent, and inadequate team communication before, during or after a shared task for 6 per cent. Of the 1,520 factors recorded for wrong surgery, a time-out that was not performed or was incomplete accounts for 10 per cent, and the shared mental model item for another 10 per cent. Of the 7,774 factors recorded for patient falls, the shared mental model item accounts for 7 per cent and inadequate staff-to-staff communication during handoffs for 6 per cent. Reporting to the Joint Commission is voluntary, and the review states that no conclusions should be drawn about the actual relative frequency of events. Direct observation gives a firmer count. Lorelei Lingard and colleagues watched 48 surgical procedures over 90 hours, involving 94 team members, and recorded 421 procedurally relevant communication events. They classed 129 of those as failures, about 30 per cent of exchanges, and 36.4 per cent of the failures had visible effects on the work, among them delay, tension, resource waste and procedural error.

replication.headline: Nobody has repeated Sasou and Reason's classification of industrial events, and the measured work sits in the adjacent literature, where the pooled link between teamwork and clinical performance is r = 0.28.
replication.detail: Jan Schmutz, Laurenz Meier and Tanja Manser pooled 31 studies covering 1,390 acute-care teams. The sample-size weighted correlation between a teamwork process and clinical performance was r = 0.28, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.35, with Q = 53.7 and I-squared of 46.0. The four studies that used patient outcomes rather than process ratings gave r = 0.13, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.23. Their test of moderators was not significant, so the relationship held across team composition, familiarity, size, task type and simulated against real patients. Ashley Hughes and colleagues meta-analysed 129 healthcare team-training studies across 146 independent samples. Training moved learning by a corrected d of 0.89, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.11, and on-the-job transfer by 0.67, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.82. The eight samples that measured medical errors gave -0.50, 95% CI -0.88 to -0.13. Angela O'Dea, Paul O'Connor and Ivan Keogh pooled 20 crew resource management evaluations in acute care and report d = 1.05 for knowledge, d = 0.22 for attitudes and d = 1.25 for behaviours, with insufficient evidence for an effect on clinical care outcomes. Amy Starmer and colleagues ran a handoff programme across nine paediatric residency programmes and 10,740 admissions. The medical-error rate fell 23 per cent, from 24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions, and preventable adverse events fell 30 per cent, from 4.7 to 3.3 per 100 admissions. Six of the nine sites showed significant error reductions. Non-preventable adverse events did not move, at 3.0 and 2.8 per 100 admissions.

limits: Sasou and Reason's paper is paywalled at Elsevier and has no repository copy in the Unpaywall record. It is quoted here from its abstract alone, read in the raw HTML of the bibliographic mirror at colab.ws. The counts of nuclear, aviation and shipping events the paper analysed are not in that abstract and are left out, as are the categories of the taxonomy itself. An application of the taxonomy to air traffic control, presented at the 2009 International Symposium on Aviation Psychology, sits behind a firewall on the host repository and was not read. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Europe PMC, PubMed, Semantic Scholar and general web search found no attempt to repeat the 1999 classification, and no published test of how reliably two coders assign the same team error category to the same event. The Joint Commission figures are shares of coded contributing factors rather than rates of events, and the underlying reports are voluntary. Schmutz and colleagues' correlation is observational, and only four of their 31 studies used patient outcomes. Hughes and colleagues' effect on errors rests on eight samples. Starmer and colleagues compared a period before their intervention with a period after it, without a control group.
misreadings: The name suggests a bias, and no laboratory demonstration stands behind it. Team error is a category in an incident taxonomy, and the entries it gets confused with are effects with experiments attached. Groupthink is a claim about decision quality flowing from concurrence seeking. Group polarisation is a claim about the direction an average moves after discussion. Team error is a claim about who gets counted when an error is traced. The second misreading is redundancy. A second pair of eyes is assumed to catch what the first missed, and Sasou and Reason's own conclusion names an excessive authority gradient and excessive professional courtesy among the causes. Sydor and colleagues put 49 anaesthesia trainees through a simulated crisis in which a consultant ordered blood for a Jehovah's Witness, with half the trainees in a hierarchical team and half not. The manipulation moved nothing. Their advocacy-inquiry scores did not differ between the groups, 92 per cent and 76 per cent of the two groups checked the blood, and 62 per cent and 57 per cent administered it. The third misreading is treating a contributing-factor table as a table of causes. A factor coded during a root cause analysis records what a reviewing team wrote down afterwards, with the outcome already known.
